title: The Compromised Badge
subtitle: Stateless JWT tokens remain valid after administrative revocation, leaking confidential files

brief.narrative: Internal Affairs discovers that Detective Vance's laptop and authentication token were stolen during an undercover bust by an organized crime syndicate. At 14:00:00, the Chief Security Officer immediately suspends Vance's credentials in the central Identity Provider (IdP) and changes his database record to `STATUS = REVOKED`. However, at 14:25:00, access logs reveal that the stolen laptop successfully downloaded 48 sealed confidential informant case files from the precinct Evidence Vault Microservice. Because the architecture uses completely stateless JSON Web Tokens (JWT) with a 12-hour expiration window (`exp`), downstream microservices validate access purely by verifying the token's RS256 signature using a cached public key. The microservices make zero calls to the IdP, oblivious to the fact that the officer was suspended. The syndicate continues harvesting state secrets using a revoked badge.
symptoms: Suspended detective account continues accessing confidential microservice endpoints 25 minutes after revocation
Evidence Vault access logs show HTTP 200 OK for requests presenting Vance's stolen JWT token
Identity Provider audit confirms Detective Vance was marked `REVOKED` at 14:00:00
Downstream microservices perform zero network lookups during JWT validation to minimize latency
brief.objective: Diagnose the architectural blindspot of stateless JWT revocation and implement short-lived access tokens with distributed in-memory revocation blocklists.

rootCause.question: What is the security root cause allowing the stolen credentials to access files after account revocation?

options.text: Stateless JWT architectural blindspot: microservices independently validate cryptographic signatures and expiration timestamps locally without real-time revocation checking, allowing stolen 12-hour tokens to remain trusted until expiration
options.feedback: Correct! Stateless JSON Web Tokens (JWT) are designed to avoid database lookups by verifying identity using public-key cryptography. However, this creates a major revocation blindspot: once issued, a token is mathematically valid until its `exp` timestamp passes. Downstream services validating only the signature and timestamp have no knowledge that the identity provider suspended the account at 14:00:00.

options.text: The RSA 2048-bit private key of the identity provider was factored by the syndicate using quantum computing
options.feedback: The private key was never compromised. The attacker did not forge a new token; they simply presented the legitimate existing token that was issued before the laptop was stolen.

options.text: A Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability on the Evidence Vault bypassed JWT validation entirely
options.feedback: The service logs show that JWT validation executed normally and passed. The failure is that the token itself was trusted despite being revoked.

options.text: The Network Time Protocol (NTP) service on the Evidence Vault drifted 24 hours into the past
options.feedback: System clocks are synchronized. The token's expiration window was 12 hours, meaning it was naturally valid for another 10+ hours under real time.

fix.question: How should the authentication architecture be redesigned to allow instantaneous revocation while maintaining high-performance microservice access?

options.text: Implement short-lived access tokens (5-minute expiry) paired with rotating refresh tokens, and broadcast revoked token IDs (jti) to an in-memory distributed Redis blocklist with pub/sub invalidation
options.feedback: Correct! A robust distributed authentication pattern combines two tiers: 1) Short-lived access tokens (e.g., 5-15 minutes) drastically shrink the window of exposure if a token is leaked. 2) For emergency revocations (stolen devices, employee termination), the IdP publishes the unique token identifier (`jti`) or user ID to an in-memory distributed cache (like Redis with Bloom filters) via pub/sub. Microservices perform a fast sub-millisecond memory lookup against the blocklist during validation, rejecting revoked tokens instantly.

options.text: Revert to monolithic server-side session cookies stored in a single relational SQL database queried synchronously on every single microservice call
options.feedback: Forcing every microservice request across dozens of internal services to hit a single relational database destroys microservice autonomy and creates a massive scalability and availability bottleneck.

options.text: Increase the JWT token expiration to 7 days so that users do not need to re-authenticate during long tactical operations
options.feedback: Extending the token expiration window to 7 days worsens the vulnerability, giving the syndicate an entire week of unrestricted access to classified systems.

options.text: Change the symmetric signing algorithm from RS256 to HS256 and distribute the secret key to all client devices
options.feedback: Distributing shared secret keys to client devices allows any client to forge arbitrary administrator tokens, completely destroying system security.
